hints.content:
The graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$ can be transformed
to get the graph of $y=3\sqrt[3]{x+6}$. 
[[☃ explanation 1]]

options.explanation:
Suppose $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$ and $g(x)=3\sqrt[3]{x+6}$.  

>$\begin{align}f(x)&=\sqrt[3]{x}\\\\
f(x+6)&=\sqrt[3]{x+6}\\\\
3f(x+6)&=3\sqrt[3]{x+6}\\\\
\end{align}$

Notice that what is on the right-hand side of the equal sign is $g(x)$.  Therefore, $g(x)=3f(x+6)$.  

Since function $g$ can be built from function $f$, the graph of function $g$ is a transformation of the graph of function $f$.

hints.content:
Replacing $x$ with $x+6$ shifts the graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$ left $6$ units.

[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: A cube root function graph and its shifted graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has a middle point at (zero, zero) and passes through (negative eight, negative two) and (eight, two). The shifted graph has a middle point at (negative six, zero) and passes through (negative fourteen, negative two) and (two, two).

hints.content:
Multiplying $\sqrt[3]{x+6}$ by $3$ stretches the graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{x+6} $ vertically by a factor of $3$.  

[[☃ image 1]]

Note that the graph of the function passes through $(2,2)$ *before* the stretch, and $(2, 6 )$ *after* the stretch.  This is because each $y$-coordinate is multiplied by $3$.  

Additionally it is important to follow order of operations when building the function, as function transformations are not always commutative.  [[☃ explanation 1]]

options.explanation:
Consider the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$.

If we shift the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ down $2$ units, and then reflect this across the $x$-axis, we get the following graph.

![A square root function graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (zero, two) and passes through (ten, negative one).](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/838d19b306cd3a25ac6c67be671bb6a26eaf0e71)

However, if we first reflect the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ across the $x$-axis and then shift this graph down $2$ units, we get the following graph.

![A square root function graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (zero, negative two) and passes through (ten, negative five).](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/76bbee52d28bfb5f5bcd72a6831a797eaab9824d)

These graphs are not the same, indicating that the order in which you perform the transformations is important!

options.alt: A cube root function graph and its vertically stretched graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has a middle point at (negative six, zero) and passes through (negative fourteen, negative two) and (two, two). The vertically stretched graph has a middle point at (negative six, zero) and passes through (negative fourteen, negative six) and (two, six).
